newsitem.title: USA: More rain seen for drenched U.S. Pacific Northwest.
newsitem.headline: More rain seen for drenched U.S. Pacific Northwest.

text.p: More rain was expected to fall in the already drenched Pacific Northwest during the next 24 to 48 hours, raising already high river levels, meteorologists said.

"Rivers are already running extremely high and this is just going to add to those problems. Some roads will be washed out due to flash floods," said meteorologist Joel Burgio of Weather Services Corp.
Burgio said rainfall should total 0.5 to 1.5 inches in Washington and Oregon with the heaviest showers in northern California where between 2.0 and 4.0 inches was expected.

In the last 24 hours western Washington and Oregon had between 0.5 and 1.0 inch of rain while eastern parts of those states had about 0.5 inch, Burgio added. He noted warm air from the Pacific was likely to restrict snow to high elevations.
Craig Solberg, meteorologist for Freese-Notis Weather, said he was forecasting more showers in the Pacific Northwest region although the outlook going into the weekend indicated drier weather.
He noted conditions contrasted with the southern Plains where there has been concern about dryness. Some rain should fall in early January after a dry December, Solberg said.
"There should be a more favorable weather pattern for wheat late this week and into next week," he said.

WSC's Burgio noted conditions in the southern Plains should be mostly fair during the next 72 hours but there was a little bit better chance of light to moderate showers late this week and into the weekend.

Highs in eastern Colorado, west and central Oklahoma and west Kansas during the next couple of days should be in the 70s Fahrenheit but temperatures should cool significantly next week to around the 40s F, he said.
"If soils warm up enough wheat could be more vulnerable to a cold snap. We are not talking about that just yet but you have to keep it in mind," WSC's Burgio said.
He said it looked as if the drop in temperatures would be gradual, limiting the threat to wheat.
